analysis.title: Decoding Datacenter Contracts: Key takeaways and transcript from our discussion with a legal expert
key_insights: Regulatory change affecting US datacenters is mostly local rather than national, driven partly by community opposition. Power availability remains the biggest near-term constraint, with community acceptance and changing local rules now also major concerns.

Value of powered land depends on timing of power: available under 12 months is a 'platinum' asset, 12-24 months 'gold', 24-48 months 'silver', and over 48 months is generally not commercially attractive.
A 400MW site can still be highly valuable if about 100MW arrives within the first 12-24 months and the rest has a credible pathway.

Large deals (over 100MW) are bespoke. Hyperscalers insist on their own lease forms, which often contain buried termination-for-convenience rights. The expert says sophisticated developers should never accept them, though they still occasionally get through.

Optionality in leases includes expansion rights for space and power, rights of first refusal, purchase options and extension options. Less sophisticated or financially pressured developers may concede these because they value the tenant's investment-grade credit and name.

Acceptable cancellation rights generally relate to loss of the power pathway or failure to meet defined development milestones. Leases may also impose delay remedies such as free-rent credits or liquidated damages, with the precise terms depending on deal size, customer type and leverage.
Neocloud deals in new development are rarely completed without a credit wrapper: upfront cash contribution, letter of credit, limited guarantee, or support from an AI or chip company.

Credit support has shifted over about the last year from full lease guarantees to limited guarantees, for example covering 80% of a construction loan but not all rent. The developer funds the equity above the construction loan. This holds across hyperscaler, AI company and chip company guarantors.

Guarantees commonly amortize straight-line over the initial lease term, so a guarantee on a 10-year lease may have little value by year 7 or 8. Guarantors increasingly seek step-in rights to take over the space and power.

Contract gotchas: a buried termination-for-convenience right, credit enhancement that is too limited or amortizes too fast, lease transfers that remove the credit support, and excessive tenant control over expansion, contraction and adjacent campus development.

The expert expects several neoclouds (probably not the largest public ones) to fail within 1-3 years because of a mismatch between a roughly 15-year datacenter lease obligation and customer contracts lasting days to months, or 1-3 years at best. He compares neoclouds to WeWork.

With strong upfront credit support, a failed neocloud tenant can leave the owner a completed facility at a lower effective basis. At $10M/MW build cost and a 30% upfront guarantee, the basis is about $7M/MW, allowing competitive remarketing if possession is recovered promptly.

The expert sees no slowdown in deal activity ('hockey stick'), with more thoughtful underwriting and more concern about becoming counterparty to a speculator. Utilities and regulators such as ERCOT (Batch Zero) are using deposits and security requirements to filter speculative power applications.

Hyperscalers now build about 20% of their capacity themselves, versus almost entirely leasing two years ago. AI companies and neoclouds do not build themselves, while many developer-owner-operators do.
Some chip manufacturers are starting to lease or own space themselves and sublease to neoclouds for more control, rather than provide credit wrappers.

One hyperscaler's credit has been questioned because of its debt load. Deals under negotiation are continuing, but new bidding contests weigh that guarantee less heavily, and worsening credit could affect deals.

Demand for smaller urban and suburban inference facilities is expected to grow over the next 3-5 years. Pricing for local capacity (250kW to 2MW) is reported up 50-100% in a couple of years as mid-sized operators were acquired, benefiting Equinix and CoreSite.
Bernstein is Outperform on MSFT, ORCL, AMT, BXDC, CSQR, DLR and EQIX, and Underperform on CRWV. The discussion was in line with its thesis.

market_movers.rationale: Bernstein says the discussion was in line with its thesis on Microsoft.
Bernstein says the discussion was in line with its thesis on Oracle.
Outperform maintained. The expert says local capacity pricing is up 50-100% and Equinix is doing very well as a result.
Outperform maintained on Blackstone Digital Infra.
Underperform maintained. The expert expects several neoclouds to fail in 1-3 years due to the lease-versus-customer-contract mismatch, and Bernstein calls itself a long-standing neocloud bear.

sector_views.rationale: No visible slowdown in deal activity and demand is expected to broaden to local inference facilities. Power timing and credit support are the key determinants of contract quality.
Lease-term mismatch with short customer contracts creates failure risk within 1-3 years, and credit wrappers are shrinking from full to partial guarantees.

risk_factors: Neocloud failures within 1-3 years from the mismatch between long datacenter leases and short customer contracts.
Guarantees that amortize linearly and cover only about 80% of construction debt leave owners with less protection over time.
Hyperscaler credit questions from rising debt, which could affect the value of their credit enhancement on new deals.
Local regulatory and community opposition changes that could alter project requirements before completion.
Power availability and timing delays, including loss of a pathway to power such as being moved out of ERCOT Batch Zero.
Buried termination-for-convenience clauses and lease transfers that eliminate credit support.
Counterparty risk from speculators in the power and datacenter market.
geopolitical: The expert cites allegations of foreign influencers behind some community opposition to datacenters in the US.

tension_points.bull_case: Strong upfront credit support (for example 30% upfront) means a failed neocloud tenant leaves the owner a built facility at about $7M/MW basis that can be remarketed competitively, while demand shows no slowdown.
tension_points.bear_case: Several neoclouds are expected to fail in 1-3 years because 15-year leases are matched against very short customer contracts, and limited guarantees that amortize linearly can be nearly worthless by year 7 or 8.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Credit support that is too limited or amortizes too fast, a lease transfer that removes the credit support, or slow recovery of possession (the expert notes New York can take 1-2 years).

theme_stances.key_argument: Neoclouds face a mismatch between long datacenter lease obligations and short customer contracts, and credit wrappers are shrinking.
theme_stances.evidence: We are long-standing neocloud bears here.

theme_stances.key_argument: Deal activity shows no slowdown and demand should broaden to smaller urban and suburban inference facilities over 3-5 years.
theme_stances.evidence: No demand slowdown: the expert reports no current slowdown in deal activity.
